rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-driven selectivity changes in either direction.
Change only gradient duration to measure the critical early pair’s sensitivity to slope. The longer gradient should spread that pair while keeping the last peak near the 10-minute scoring threshold.
The critical pair improved only modestly with a shallower gradient, so test temperature-driven selectivity at the original slope. Higher temperature should also preserve the favorable last-peak time.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness at the temperature that nearly resolved the critical pair. This should raise its resolution above 1.5 while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes, targeting the maximum CRF of 1.0.

The maximum CRF is secured; now seek a shorter fully resolved run. This gradient has a slope between injections 3 and 4, which should retain R ≥ 1.5 for the critical pair while shortening the last-peak time.

Shift the starting organic fraction upward while keeping the slope close to injection 5, testing whether the elution window can be shortened without losing early-pair resolution. The endpoint remains well above the estimated organic fraction at the last peak.

Restore the lower starting fraction that favors the critical pair, with a slope predicted to keep its resolution just above 1.5. The last peak may elute briefly into the final hold, testing a shorter program without approaching the acquisition limit.

With CRF 1.0 secured, explore whether lower temperature reverses the critical pair’s selectivity enough to tolerate a faster gradient. The broad, steep gradient should limit late retention while testing a potentially shorter fully resolved method.

Keep the low-temperature selectivity that resolved the early pair and reduce the slope to test whether the late three-peak cluster separates. Comparing directly with injection 8 will reveal whether this alternative temperature regime can support full resolution.

The late cluster barely responded to gradient duration at 25 C, indicating temperature is the better selectivity lever. Raising temperature one step tests whether that cluster opens while retaining the strong early-pair resolution.

Test an intermediate temperature to separate the late cluster, with a higher starting organic fraction and shorter gradient to reduce retention time. This explores whether changing the starting window preserves enough early-pair selectivity for a faster fully resolved method.

Return to the successful high-temperature regime and test whether a shallower, shifted gradient restores early-pair resolution at a higher starting organic fraction. This probes the trade-off between removing initial low-organic time and spreading the critical pair.

Back off the starting organic fraction from injection 12 and use a shallower slope than injection 6 to recover early-pair resolution. This tests a compact gradient window as an alternative maximum-score method.

Increase the slope slightly relative to injection 13 to test its early-pair resolution boundary and shorten the last-peak time. The higher endpoint keeps all peaks within the gradient; resolution is expected to remain close to 1.5.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 7 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary at 60 C. The early pair is expected to be near R = 1.5, with the last peak slightly earlier and entirely within the gradient.

Explore a higher starting fraction at 35 C, where the early pair has different selectivity from the successful 60 C methods. A shallower slope than injection 11 may resolve both critical regions while the shifted window keeps the last peak early.

Lowering the starting fraction from injection 16 should restore early retention, while a shallower slope than injection 11 should improve its critical pair. This tests a fully resolved, lower-temperature alternative expected to keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Back off from injection 15’s slightly excessive slope to recover full early-pair resolution. This should give a last-peak time near 7 minutes with a little more resolution margin than injection 7 and all peaks inside the gradient.

Test a shorter programmed gradient with a slope slightly shallower than the fully resolved injection 13. The final hold should elute the last compound without approaching the acquisition limit, while checking whether this compact program preserves maximum CRF.

The fastest fully resolved candidate remains injection 7; use this injection to seek greater resolution margin without sacrificing the maximum score. A shallower gradient should strengthen the early pair, while monitoring the third–fourth pair and keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Seek a shorter maximum-score method with more resolution margin than the fastest candidates. This slope lies between injections 13 and 20, while the higher starting fraction should help preserve separation of the third–fourth pair.

Increase the slope from injection 20 to shorten its last-peak time and improve the third–fourth pair, while retaining ample early-pair resolution. This targets a maximum-score method with balanced resolution margins between the two limiting pairs.

Steepen injection 22 by one endpoint step to shorten the run while retaining predicted full resolution. This should provide an intermediate option between its larger resolution margin and the faster, near-threshold methods.

Shorten the gradient from injection 21 by increasing its endpoint, targeting full resolution near the boundary established by injection 14. This should retain CRF 1.0 with the last peak around 7.2 minutes and slightly more early-pair margin than injection 14.

Use the same starting fraction, temperature, and gradient slope as maximum-score injection 4, but trim the endpoint and programmed duration. All peaks should remain within the gradient, preserving full resolution and a last-peak time near 7.5 minutes.
